title: Pentagon's Iran War Bill Tops $43 Billion as Stockpile Drain and Political Firestorm Intensify
snippet: U.S. Central Command reports that military spending in the Iran conflict has reached $43.6 billion, raising concerns over depleted global missile stockpiles and sparking sharp political battles on Capitol Hill.
content:
WASHINGTON — The financial cost of the war in Iran has surged past $43.6 billion, according to Pentagon figures provided to congressional national security committees, illustrating the staggering economic and operational toll of the ongoing conflict.

However, defense officials acknowledge the true price tag is likely far higher. The updated figures, compiled by U.S. Central Command through Sept. 3, omit the extensive costs required to repair damaged or destroyed American bases across the Middle East, including a crucial U.S. Navy logistics facility in Bahrain struck by Iranian fire.

Stockpiles Dwindle as Human Toll Rises

The vast majority of the war's budget has been swallowed by munitions replacement. The Pentagon estimates spending $28.1 billion to restock precision bombs and advanced air defense interceptors since joint U.S. and Israeli airstrikes began on Feb. 28. Defense analysts caution that the sustained pace of fire is severely exhausting critical weapons reserves, leaving the U.S. potentially vulnerable in other strategic theaters, including the Indo-Pacific.

Beyond the financial toll, the human cost continues to climb. More than 50,000 U.S. troops are presently deployed within Central Command's operational footprint. Official reports confirm at least 18 American service members have been killed and over 800 wounded since hostilities erupted.

Branch Breakdown and Capitol Hill Backlash

Individual service costs highlight the heavy operational tempo. The Air Force has spent $6.6 billion—a total that accounts for the loss of dozens of aircraft—while the Navy has expended $2.2 billion deploying multiple aircraft carrier strike groups and over two dozen warships. Ground operations have cost the Army an additional $1.6 billion.

The spiraling expenses have accelerated political friction in Washington. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., recently filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging the administration violated constitutional limits by waging war without explicit congressional authorization. House leadership temporarily paused legislative sessions to avoid an immediate floor vote on the measure.

Critics on both sides of the aisle have grown increasingly vocal. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., blasted the administration's military oversight, arguing that management failures are placing strain on national readiness while imposing massive financial burdens on American taxpayers.
